before_text.title: Josef Kates
before_text.subtitle: Engineer and early game-computing pioneer
before_text.summary: Josef Kates was a Canadian engineer whose work includes Bertie the Brain and automated traffic signalling.
body: Josef Kates, born Josef Katz, (May 5, 1921 – June 16, 2018) was a Canadian engineer whose achievements include designing the first digital game-playing machine, and the world's first automated traffic signalling system.

Born the fifth of six children in an Austrian-Jewish family, Josef Kates was the son of Baruch (Bernard) and Anna Katz (née Entenberg). His parents ran a grocery store and an import-export business in Vienna. Kates fled to Italy to escape the Nazis after the Anschluss in 1938 and then, in 1939, joined the rest of his family which had fled to England. Kates enlisted in the British Army but, before he could see service, he and other Germans and Austrians resident in Britain were interned as enemy aliens. Kates was deported to Canada where he remained interned for almost two years until he and most of his fellow Jewish internees were recognised by the government as "victims of Nazi aggression" and released. At the camps in New Brunswick and Quebec, Kates fished, worked as a lumberjack, knitted socks and studied for his high school diploma through McGill University's high school matriculation program, placing first in Quebec's province-wide exams.  After his release in 1942, he moved to Toronto where he met Lillian Kroch, marrying her in 1944.  They had four children: Louis, Naomi, Celina and Philip A.

He was educated at Goethe-Realschule (Vienna: 1931–1938); McGill University (Montreal: 1941, junior and senior matriculation); University of Toronto (Toronto: 1944–1948, Honours in Mathematics and Physics; 1948-1949: M.A. in Applied Math; 1949-1951: Ph.D. in physics).

Kates started his career working for the Imperial Optical Company of Toronto in 1942, and was in charge of precision optics for Royal Canadian Navy equipment until he left in 1944. He then spent time working for Rogers Vacuum Tube Company, (now Royal Philips Electronics), for the next four years in the development and manufacturing of radar and radio tubes.  He then began work in 1948 at the University of Toronto Computation Centre, where he participated in the design and building of UTEC, the first pilot model of a computer built in Canada.

Kates also built the first digital game playing machine, the 13-foot tall Bertie the Brain, which was exhibited at the 1950 Canadian National Exhibition. The game was a version of Tic-tac-toe, with adjustable difficulty levels. The game machine controlled the lighting of an overhead display to show the progress of the game, and was built using a special electron tube, the Additron Tube, which Kates had invented. The Additron Tube did the work of ten existing radio tubes, reducing the size and complexity of the machine.  With the advent of transistors, which were much smaller and required less power, the tube was not put into commercial use.
Kates also designed Toronto's automated traffic signalling system in 1954 - the first in the world.

Kates founded and became the President of KCS Ltd in Toronto between 1954 and 1966, which merged with the consulting arm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co. to become Kates, Peat, Marwick & Co. in Canada, with other corporations in the US and the UK, for which he acted as a co-managing partner.  He served as a computer consultant to many Canadian and American firms and organizations. He was involved in the creation of Setak Computer Services Corp. Ltd. (his last name spelled backwards) which was based in Toronto; it offered computer access and consulting based on Burroughs computers, e.g. the B5500. Setak's employee Barry W. Ramer later went on to found Barry W. Ramer & Partners Ltd. and Ramer Data Consulting Ltd. Management Consulting in Calgary Alberta. In 1974 he founded Josef Kates Associates Inc., for which he acted as president.

In 1968, he was appointed to the Science Council of Canada, and served as its chairman from 1975 to 1978. Kates was also chairman, CEO and director of Teleride Sage Ltd. (1977–1996), and IRD Teleride (1996–1997) followed until his retirement.
In 2014, at the age of 93, Kates designed a proposed improvement for Toronto Transit Commission subway system.
His wife, Lillian Kroch, died of cancer in 1993 after almost 50 years of marriage. In 1995, Kates married his second wife, Kay Hill. Kates died in Toronto on June 16, 2018.

before_text.title: Ralph Baer
before_text.subtitle: A life in games
before_text.summary: Ralph Baer developed television-game prototypes that led to the Magnavox Odyssey.
body: Ralph Henry Baer (born Rudolf Heinrich Baer; March 8, 1922 – December 6, 2014) was a German-born American inventor, game developer, and engineer.

Baer's Jewish family fled Germany just before World War II and Baer served the American war effort, gaining an interest in electronics shortly thereafter. Through several jobs in the electronics industry, he was working as an engineer at Sanders Associates (now BAE Systems) in Nashua, New Hampshire, when he conceived the idea of playing games on a television screen around 1966. With support of his employers, he worked through several prototypes until he arrived at a "Brown Box" that would later become the blueprint for the first home video game console, licensed by Magnavox as the Magnavox Odyssey. Baer continued to design several other consoles and computer game units, including contributing to design of the Simon electronic game. Baer continued to work in electronics until his death in 2014, with over 150 patents to his name.

Baer is considered "the Father of Video Games" due to his many contributions to games and helping to spark the video game industry in the latter half of the 20th century. In February 2006, he was awarded the National Medal of Technology for "his groundbreaking and pioneering creation, development and commercialization of interactive video games, which spawned related uses, applications, and mega-industries in both the entertainment and education realms".
story_headings: Television games take shape in the 1960s

before_text.title: Yu Suzuki
before_text.subtitle: Yu Suzuki Uses Technology to Make Speed, Space and Everyday Life Physical
before_text.summary: Yu Suzuki connected arcade hardware, character animation and the everyday rhythms of Shenmue. His career spans Sega's simulation cabinets, Virtua Fighter and YS Net.
body: Yu Suzuki joined Sega in 1983 after studying electronic science at Okayama University of Science. Hang-On and Space Harrier followed in 1985. These were games whose machines mattered as much as their screens: motorcycle controls, moving cabinets and rapidly scaled scenery made movement something a player could feel. Space Harrier placed that sense of speed in a strange fantasy landscape rather than on a recognisable road.

Out Run offered a different kind of journey. Suzuki researched European roads, and the game turned driving into a succession of changing landscapes and branching routes. The player raced a clock rather than a championship table. Hiroshi Kawaguchi's music was part of that identity: choosing a radio track before setting off helped give the drive its relaxed, aspirational character. The route and the soundtrack made the same car feel like a personal escape.

In Sega's twentieth-anniversary interview, Suzuki traced Virtua Fighter back to the pit crew in Virtua Racing. After rendering cars, he wanted to animate a human body with many connected joints. The hardware could not handle a whole football or rugby team, so he narrowed the problem to two people. That technical constraint met the arcade market's interest in fighting games. Virtua Fighter emerged from both questions, rather than simply putting polygons over an existing formula.

Shenmue moved Suzuki's work from the short arcade session into a neighbourhood the player could inhabit. Ryo Hazuki investigated his father's murder in Yokosuka, but progress also involved waiting for a shop to open, asking residents for directions or earning money at the harbour. Daily schedules and changing weather helped the setting feel independent of the investigation. Martial-arts fights and timed action sequences shared space with ordinary routines.

Shenmue II continued Ryo's search in Hong Kong before taking him to Kowloon and Guilin. The move widened the first game's scale: crowded streets, unfamiliar districts and new companions replaced the familiarity of his home neighbourhood. The story still depended on conversations, work, exploration and martial arts. Its larger setting also made navigation part of the experience; learning how to find someone was a task in its own right.

Suzuki founded YS Net in 2008. In 2015, a Kickstarter campaign gave Shenmue III a route back into production after the long gap since the second game. It was released in 2019, continuing Ryo and Shenhua's story in rural China. The circumstances were different from Sega's Dreamcast era: a new studio and a community of backers helped carry the continuation. Suzuki also received the Golden Joystick Lifetime Achievement award that year.

1993 / From a pit crew to two fighters
2008–2019 / Building YS Net and returning to Shenmue

before_text.title: Roberta Williams
before_text.subtitle: What if the room had a picture?
before_text.summary: Roberta Williams took the places of a text adventure and made players look at them as well as read about them.
body: A text adventure asks a player to construct a place from sentences. Roberta Williams saw another possibility. In Mystery House, the player would still type commands and read responses, but a drawing would also show the location. A computer mystery could give its audience something to examine on the screen.

Williams designed the game and its story; Ken Williams built the software that brought it to the Apple II. Released through On-Line Systems in 1980, Mystery House used spare line drawings rather than the detailed paintings that later adventure games would make familiar. Those limits are visible, but so is the decision that mattered. Images became part of how a player understood a room, followed a mystery and imagined what might be waiting elsewhere.

Making the picture did not remove the need for language. Players still had to decide what an object meant and how to express an action. Looking and typing became connected activities. The drawing could establish a place immediately, while the words could explain what the drawing could not.

Williams continued exploring these relationships in games including King's Quest. As the hardware changed, the rooms became more elaborate and characters could move through them. The through-line is a designer choosing how to let someone enter a story. Before a graphical world could feel inhabited, somebody had to decide that an adventure should show its rooms.

before_text.title: Ralph Baer, Bill Harrison and Bill Rusch
before_text.subtitle: Making television answer back
before_text.summary: The Brown Box prototypes imagined a television as something a household could play with.
body: Working at Sanders Associates, Ralph Baer and colleagues Bill Harrison and Bill Rusch developed a sequence of television-game prototypes. The wood-grain-covered Brown Box could support several games rather than one fixed activity. A light gun was among the team's experimental accessories.

Magnavox licensed the technology and released the Odyssey in 1972. Baer's surviving notebooks, prototypes and workshop make this more than a story about one successful object: they preserve decisions, failed paths and the collaboration behind it.
story_headings: Following the work behind the object
